claim: Vertebrates can change their behavior upon detection of visual stimuli according to the outcome their actions produce.
source: Vertebrates can change their behavior upon detection of visual stimuli according to the outcome their actions produce.
evidence: This is a general statement about vertebrate behavior that draws from established scientific understanding.

claim: Goal-directed behavior involves evolutionary conserved brain structures like the striatum and optic tectum, which receive ascending visual input from the periphery.
source: Such goal-directed behavior involves evolutionary conserved brain structures like the striatum and optic tectum, which receive ascending visual input from the periphery.
evidence: This statement draws from established neuroscience knowledge about brain structures involved in goal-directed behavior.

claim: In mammals, the striatum and optic tectum receive descending visual input from visual cortex via neurons that give rise to cortico-fugal projections.
source: In mammals, however, these structures also receive descending visual input from visual cortex (VC), via neurons that give rise to cortico-fugal projections.
evidence: This statement draws from established anatomical knowledge about mammalian brain connectivity.

claim: The ablation of striatal projecting neurons reduces learning speed in a visual detection task.
source: We show that the ablation of striatal projecting neurons reduces learning speed, whereas the ablation of superior colliculus projecting neurons does not impact learning but reduces detection sensitivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing behavioral effects of CSt neuron ablation.

claim: The ablation of superior colliculus projecting neurons does not impact learning but reduces detection sensitivity.
source: We show that the ablation of striatal projecting neurons reduces learning speed, whereas the ablation of superior colliculus projecting neurons does not impact learning but reduces detection sensitivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing behavioral effects of CT neuron ablation.

claim: The striatum is fundamental for reinforcement learning.
source: The striatum is fundamental for reinforcement learning (Cox and Witten, 2019) and action initiation (Klaus et al., 2019) and the optic tectum (called the superior colliculus in mammals) plays an important role in the detection of salient visual stimuli that trigger innate behaviors (Feinberg and Mallatt, 2019; Grillner and El Manira, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The striatum is fundamental for action initiation.
source: The striatum is fundamental for reinforcement learning (Cox and Witten, 2019) and action initiation (Klaus et al., 2019) and the optic tectum (called the superior colliculus in mammals) plays an important role in the detection of salient visual stimuli that trigger innate behaviors (Feinberg and Mallatt, 2019; Grillner and El Manira, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The optic tectum (called the superior colliculus in mammals) plays an important role in the detection of salient visual stimuli that trigger innate behaviors.
source: The striatum is fundamental for reinforcement learning (Cox and Witten, 2019) and action initiation (Klaus et al., 2019) and the optic tectum (called the superior colliculus in mammals) plays an important role in the detection of salient visual stimuli that trigger innate behaviors (Feinberg and Mallatt, 2019; Grillner and El Manira, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Mammals are able to learn and perform simple sensory detection tasks even in the absence of sensory neocortex.
source: In fact, mammals are able to learn and perform simple sensory detection tasks even in the absence of sensory neocortex (Ceballo et al., 2019; Dalmay et al., 2019; Hong et al., 2018; Pöppel et al., 1973; Popper and Fay, 1992; Weiskrantz et al., 1974).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Distinct populations of neurons in VC send visual information to the dorso-medial striatum (dmSt) and the superior colliculus (SC) via two prominent cortico-fugal pathways, the cortico-striatal (CSt) and the cortico-tectal (CT), respectively.
source: Distinct populations of neurons in VC send visual information to the dorso-medial striatum (dmSt) and the superior colliculus (SC; the mammalian optic tectum) via two prominent cortico-fugal pathways, the cortico-striatal (CSt; Faull et al., 1986; Kemp and Powell, 1970; Khibnik et al., 2014; Saint-Cyr et al., 1990) and the cortico-tectal (CT; Wang and Burkhalter, 2013; Zingg et al., 2017), respectively (Hattox and Nelson, 2007; Jones, 1984; Lur et al., 2016; Norita et al., 1991; Rhoades et al., 1985; Serizawa et al., 1994; Swadlow, 1983; Tang and Higley, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Learning was characterized by a gradual increase in the aROC with a linear fit from day 1 to day 14 showing aROC/day: 0.028 ± 0.003.
source: Learning was characterized by a gradual increase in the aROC (linear fit from day 1 to day 14 aROC/day: 0.028 ± 0.003; mean ± SEM; N = 8 mice; population average slope aROC/day: 0.030 ± 0.023; mean ±RMSE, R2 = 0.9584, p<0.001; F-test), by a progressive reduction in first lick latency and a reduction in the trial-to-trial variability of the first lick latency on stimulus trials (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral training experiments.

claim: Learning was completed on average by the 14th day of training with an aROC of 0.86 ± 0.04.
source: On average learning was completed by the 14th day of training (aROC 0.86 ± 0.04; first lick latency 0.52 ± 0.13 s; variability:0.12 ± 0.05 s; mean ± SEM; N = 8 mice).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral training experiments.

claim: CT and CSt neurons represent distinct populations in VC with an overlap of less than 3.4%.
source: Using the retrograde tracer Cholera toxin B (CTB; Luppi et al., 1990; Wan et al., 1982), we verified that CT and CSt neurons indeed represent distinct populations in VC (overlap <3.4%; 107 of 3187 CTB-labeled cells; 4.62 ± 1.13% of the CSt and 8.82 ± 4.88% of the CT population; Figure 1—figure supplement 3), consistent with previous reports (Brown and Hestrin, 2009; Lur et al., 2016; Norita et al., 1991; Serizawa et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using retrograde tracing and is consistent with cited previous reports.

claim: The vast majority of CT and CSt neurons were located in layer 5.
source: The vast majority of CT and CSt neurons were located in layer 5 and, while the two populations of neurons largely intermingled, CT neurons tended to be more tightly distributed toward the lower part of the layer (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The efficiency of retroAAV-Cre in retrogradely labeling cortico-fugal neurons was similar to CTB.
source: The efficiency of retroAAV-Cre in retrogradely labeling cortico-fugal neurons was similar to CTB (retroAAV-Cre: 30 ± 14 cells/100 µm3; retrograde tracer CTB: 24 ± 9 cells/100 µm3 in layer 5; mean ± SD; N = 3 mice).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing retroAAV-Cre and CTB labeling efficiency.

claim: The retroAAV-Cre was highly efficient as the majority of CTB-labeled cells co-expressed nuclear mCherry (85.5%, 864 cells of 1010, N = 2 mice).
source: The retroAAV-Cre was highly efficient as the majority of CTB-labeled cells co-expressed nuclear mCherry (85.5%, 864 cells of 1010, N = 2 mice; Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The viral ablation of Cre recombinase expressing CT neurons in VC was highly efficient with over 90% of ablated neurons 3 weeks after the injection.
source: The viral ablation of Cre recombinase expressing CT neurons in VC was highly efficient with over 90% of ablated neurons 3 weeks after the injection, as verified histologically (retroAAV-Cre only: 26 ± 8 cells/100 µm3 in layer 5 vs. retroAAV-Cre and AAV-taCasp3: 1 ± 1 cells/100 µm3 in layer 5; mean ± SD; N = 3 mice; p<0.001 Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A.

claim: Ablation of CT neurons had little impact on task learning as compared to controls.
source: Ablation of CT neurons had little impact on task learning as compared to controls in which only the retroAAV-Cre had been injected (aROC/day CT-ablation: 0.03 ± 0.006 vs. retroAAV-Cre only: 0.03 ± 0.004; mean ± SEM; N = 5 mice, n.s. Mann-Whitney U test; population average CT-ablation slope aROC/day: 0.029 ± 0.0014 vs. retroAAV-Cre only slope aROC/day: 0.026 ± 0.001; mean ±RMSE; n.s.; Fisher z-test; Figure 1D and Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing CT-ablated and control animals.

claim: By the 14th day of training, CT-ablated mice reached an aROC similar to control animals (CT-ablation aROC:0.85 ± 0.08 vs. retroAAV-Cre only aROC 0.84 ± 0.04).
source: Accordingly, by the 14th day of training, CT-ablated mice reached an aROC similar to controls animals (CT-ablation aROC:0.85 ± 0.08 vs. retroAAV-Cre only aROC 0.84 ± 0.04; mean ± SEM; n.s. Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing CT-ablated and control animals.

claim: The ablation of cortico-fugal neurons that project to the SC has no effect on the acquisition of the task.
source: Thus, the ablation cortico-fugal neurons that project to the SC has no effect on the acquisition of the task.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on CT neuron ablation.

claim: In CSt-ablated mice the visual specificity of the licking behavior increased much slower than in control and CT-ablated mice.
source: In striking contrast to control and CT-ablated mice, in CSt-ablated mice the visual specificity of the licking behavior increased much slower (aROC/day CSt-ablation: 0.014 ± 0.003 vs. retroAAV-Cre only: 0.03 ± 0.004; mean ± SEM; p<0.05; Mann-Whitney U test; population average CSt-ablation slope aROC/day: 0.014 ± 0.0018 vs. retroAAV-Cre only slope aROC/day: 0.026 ± 0.001; mean ±RMSE; Fisher z-test; p<0.001; CSt-ablation slope aROC/day: 0.014 ± 0.0018 vs. CT-ablation slope aROC/day: 0.029 ± 0.0014; mean ±RMSE; Fisher z-test; p<0.001; Figure 1E and Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing CSt-ablated, CT-ablated, and control animals.

claim: By day 14 of training, CSt-ablated mice had an aROC of only 0.68 ± 0.04 compared with 0.84 ± 0.04 in control animals.
source: As a consequence, by day 14 of training, CSt-ablated mice had an aROC of only 0.68 ± 0.04 compared with 0.84 ± 0.04 in control animals in which only the retroAAV-Cre had been injected (p<0.001 Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing CSt-ablated and control animals.

claim: The spontaneous lick frequency was similar between control and CSt-ablated mice across the 2 weeks of training.
source: The spontaneous lick frequency was similar between control and CSt-ablated mice across the 2 weeks of training (inter-lick-interval: intact: 1.29 ± 0.03 s; retroAAV-Cre control: 1.27 ± 0.03 s vs. 1.40 ± 0.04 s mean ± SEM; n.s.; Mann-Whitney U test, Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing spontaneous licking behavior.

claim: The number of trials performed during the training period was similar in CSt-ablated and control mice.
source: In addition, the impairments in task learning was not due to a decrease in the number of trials the animals performed during the training period neither to a reduced spontaneous lick frequency because these behavioral variables were similar in CSt-ablated and control mice (number of trials per training session: intact: 242.5 ± 3.2; retroAAV-Cre only: 232.8 ± 2.6 vs. CSt-ablation: 237.6 ± 5.3; mean ± SEM, n.s. Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing trial numbers.

claim: Ablation of cortico-fugal neurons that project to the dmSt led to slower learning such that by 2 weeks of training, learning was still incomplete.
source: Thus, ablation of cortico-fugal neurons that project to the dmSt led to slower learning such that by 2 weeks of training, learning was still incomplete.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on CSt neuron ablation.

claim: VC lesions led to slower learning as compared to intact animals.
source: Like in CSt-ablated animals, VC lesions led to slower learning (population average VC lesion slope aROC/day: 0.014 ± 0.0014 vs. CSt ablation slope aROC/day: 0.014 ± 0.0018; mean ±RMSE; n.s.; Fisher z-test) as compared to intact animals (VC lesion slope aROC/day: 0.014 ± 0.0014 vs. control slope aROC/day: 0.025 ± 0.0014; mean ±RMSE; p<0.001 Fisher z-test) such that by 2 weeks of training none of the VC-lesioned mice reached criterion (VC lesion: aROC of 0.60 ± 0.03 vs. intact: 0.86 ± 0.04; mean ± SEM; p=0.0040; Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing VC-lesioned and intact animals.

claim: VC lesions recapitulate the effect of CSt neuron ablation.
source: Thus, VC lesions recapitulate the effect of CSt neuron ablation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the effects of VC lesions and CSt neuron ablation.

claim: Ablation of CSt neurons impairs learning speed.
source: These results indicate that ablation of CSt neurons impairs learning speed.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on CSt neuron ablation.

claim: By the 14th day of training, intact animals had reached the learning criterion while CSt-ablated and VC-ablated animals were still below criterion.
source: As described above, by the 14th day of training, intact animals had reached the learning criterion while CSt-ablated and VC-ablated animals were still below criterion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing different groups of animals.

claim: By the 14th day of training, intact animals had reached plateau because further training did not improve their performance.
source: Importantly, by the 14th day of training, intact animals had reached plateau because further training did not improve their performance (slope aROC/day 2.46 × 10−4 ± 0.021; mean ±RMSE; R2 = 9.51 × 10−4, n.s.; F-test; population average linear fit from day 14 to day 21; Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no further improvement in intact animals.

claim: Both CSt-ablated and VC-lesioned animals continued to improve in the visual specificity of their licking behavior with additional training.
source: In striking contrast to the plateau performance of intact animals, both CSt-ablated and VC-lesioned animals continued to improve in the visual specificity of their licking behavior with additional training (CSt-ablation lesion slope aROC/day 0.033 ± 0.054, mean ±RMSE; R2 = 0.83, F-test; p<0.001; VC lesion slope aROC/day 0.022 ± 0.063, mean ±RMSE; R2 = 0.78, F-test; p<0.001; Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing continued improvement in CSt-ablated and VC-lesioned animals.

claim: By the end of the third week, CSt-ablated and VC-ablated animals reached an aROC similar to the plateau levels of control animals.
source: By the end of the third week, CSt-ablated and VC-ablated animals reached an aROC of 0.87 ± 0.02 and 0.76 ± 0.05, hence similar to the plateau levels of control animals (intact aROC: 0.84 ± 0.03 vs. VC-lesion: 0.76 ± 0.05; n.s.; retroAAV-Cre only: 0.81 ± 0.05 vs. CSt-ablation: 0.87 ± 0.02 n.s., Mann-Whitney U test; Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing performance after extended training.

claim: Mice that had learned the task before VC lesion maintained a high visual specificity of the licking behavior even after VC lesions.
source: Strikingly, mice that had learned the task before VC lesion maintained a high visual specificity of the licking behavior even after VC lesions (aROC pre-lesion: 0.92 ± 0.02 vs. aROC post-lesion: 0.91 ± 0.08, mean ± SEM; N = 5 mice, n.s. Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing performance before and after VC lesion in trained animals.

claim: Once learning has occurred, CSt neurons are no longer required for the animal's ability to execute the task.
source: Thus, once learning has occurred, CSt neurons are no longer required for the animal's ability to execute the task.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing maintained performance after VC lesion in trained animals.

claim: Optogenetic silencing of VC did not impair performance in response to stimuli presented at full contrast.
source: Consistent with the above results in which we surgically removed VC, optogenetic silencing of VC did not impair performance in response to stimuli presented at full contrast (aROC control: 0.88 ± 0.02 vs. aROC VC Silencing: 0.90 ± 0.04; mean ± SEM; N = 6 mice, n.s. Wilcoxon signed rank test; Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using optogenetic silencing.

claim: At lower contrasts, silencing VC significantly reduced performance leading to a rightward shift of the psychometric function and a corresponding increase in the contrast threshold for detection.
source: However, at lower contrasts, silencing VC significantly reduced performance leading to a rightward shift of the psychometric function and a corresponding increase in the contrast threshold for detection (threshold contrast: control 7.8 ± 1% vs. VC silencing: 28 ± 3%, Weibull fit; see Materials and methods, p<0.01 Wilcoxon signed rank test; Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using optogenetic silencing at different contrast levels.

claim: VC modulates sensitivity by lowering the contrast threshold for stimulus detection.
source: Thus, VC modulates sensitivity by lowering the contrast threshold for stimulus detection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on VC silencing effects on contrast detection.

claim: Upon ablation of CT neurons the acute silencing of VC no longer lead to an increase in the detection threshold.
source: Strikingly, upon ablation of CT neurons the acute silencing of VC no longer lead to an increase in the detection threshold (pre CT-ablation: threshold contrast: control 13.9 ± 3.3% vs. VC silencing: 35.4 ± 5.4%, p<0.05; post CT-ablation: threshold contrast: control 25.8 ± 9.5% vs. VC silencing: 31.2 ± 15.8%, N = 3 mice; n.s. Wilcoxon signed rank test; Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing VC silencing effects before and after CT neuron ablation.

claim: Cortico-fugal neurons projecting to the SC, while not involved in learning, increase detection sensitivity and thus enhances an animal's ability to detect less salient stimuli.
source: These data indicate that cortico-fugal neurons projecting to the SC, while not involved in learning, increase detection sensitivity and thus enhances an animal's ability to detect less salient stimuli.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on CT neuron function.

claim: Animals trained 2–7 weeks showed a strong rightward shift in the psychometric function and an increase in detection threshold of approximately 3.4-fold upon VC silencing.
source: Interestingly, while animals trained 2–7 weeks (31 ± 12 days median ± SD; N = 6 mice) showed a strong rightward shift in the psychometric function and an increase in detection threshold of approximately 3.4-fold upon VC silencing (threshold contrast: control 7.75 ± 1.8%, VC silencing: 26.6 ± 5.0%, p<0.01; Wilcoxon signed rank test; N = 6 mice; Figure 6A), detection sensitivity of animals trained 10–17 weeks (93 ± 9 days, median ± SD; N = 4 mice) was much less affected by VC silencing as the detection threshold upon VC silencing increased only 1.5 times (threshold contrast: control 10.02 ± 2.1%, VC silencing.: 15.5 ± 3.7%, n.s.; Wilcoxon signed rank test; Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing VC silencing effects at different training durations.

claim: Detection sensitivity of animals trained 10–17 weeks was much less affected by VC silencing as the detection threshold upon VC silencing increased only 1.5 times.
source: Interestingly, while animals trained 2–7 weeks (31 ± 12 days median ± SD; N = 6 mice) showed a strong rightward shift in the psychometric function and an increase in detection threshold of approximately 3.4-fold upon VC silencing (threshold contrast: control 7.75 ± 1.8%, VC silencing: 26.6 ± 5.0%, p<0.01; Wilcoxon signed rank test; N = 6 mice; Figure 6A), detection sensitivity of animals trained 10–17 weeks (93 ± 9 days, median ± SD; N = 4 mice) was much less affected by VC silencing as the detection threshold upon VC silencing increased only 1.5 times (threshold contrast: control 10.02 ± 2.1%, VC silencing.: 15.5 ± 3.7%, n.s.; Wilcoxon signed rank test; Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing VC silencing effects at different training durations.

claim: The impact of VC on detection sensitivity diminishes with training.
source: Thus, the impact of VC on detection sensitivity diminishes with training (Pearson correlation coefficient R = −0.612; p=0.013; R2 = 0.37; N = 16 mice; Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing correlation between training duration and VC impact.

claim: Early in training, VC silencing robustly reduced visual responses in the cortical recipient layers of SC, namely the stratum opticum and stratum griseum intermediale, and less so in the retino-recipient layer.
source: Early in training, VC silencing robustly reduced visual responses in the cortical recipient layers of SC, namely the stratum opticum and stratum griseum intermediale, and less so in the retino-recipient layer (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from electrophysiological recordings in SC.

claim: Later in training, visual responses across SC layers were less dependent on VC input.
source: Later in training, visual responses across SC layers were less dependent on VC input (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from electrophysiological recordings in SC at different training stages.

claim: The impact of the CT neurons both on detection sensitivity and on visual-evoked activity in the SC diminishes progressively with prolonged training.
source: Thus, the impact of the CT neurons both on detection sensitivity and on visual-evoked activity in the SC diminishes progressively with prolonged training.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on CT neuron function over training.

claim: VC, via the CSt neurons, plays a crucial role in the speed at which an animal learns to report the presence of visual stimuli.
source: On the one hand, VC, via the CSt neurons, plays a crucial role in the speed at which an animal learns to report the presence of visual stimuli.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on CSt neuron function.

claim: Once the task has been learned VC modulates detection sensitivity via the CT neurons.
source: On the other hand, once the task has been learned VC modulates detection sensitivity via the CT neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on CT neuron function.

claim: Eventually, both populations of cortico-fugal neurons become dispensable for the task.
source: Furthermore, eventually, both populations of cortico-fugal neurons become dispensable for the task.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing reduced impact of VC with prolonged training.

claim: Neurons projecting to the dmSt play their main role during the acquisition phase of the detection task.
source: Neurons projecting to the dmSt play their main role during the acquisition phase of the detection task as the ablation of CSt neurons impairs the learning speed but not the animal's ability to detect salient visual stimuli once the task has been learned.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on CSt neuron function.

claim: The finding that VC via CSt neurons plays a preferential role during learning is reminiscent of the necessity of motor cortex in the learning but not for the performance of some motor tasks.
source: The finding that VC via CSt neurons plays a preferential role during learning is reminiscent of the necessity of motor cortex in the learning but not for the performance of some motor tasks (Kawai et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim draws a comparison to previous research on motor cortex function.

claim: CSt neurons may function as a tutor to mediate learning-related plasticity in subcortical circuits that underlie the performance of the task.
source: Given that the elimination of CSt neurons once the task has been learned does not affect performance, CSt neurons may function as a tutor to mediate learning-related plasticity in subcortical circuits that underlie the performance of the task.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The plastic events that occur during learning, while relying on the CSt input, do not reside at the CSt synapse.
source: Our data suggest that the plastic events that occur during learning, while relying on the CSt input, do not reside at the CSt synapse. Otherwise removing VC after learning would impair performance.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing maintained performance after VC removal in trained animals.

claim: The ability of neurons in sensory cortex to encode specific spatial and temporal features of the stimulus may likely be the neural basis for the role of VC in feature discrimination tasks.
source: The ability of neurons in sensory cortex to encode specific spatial and temporal features of the stimulus may likely be the neural basis for the role of VC (Glickfeld et al., 2013; Jurjut et al., 2017; Marques et al., 2018; Petruno et al., 2013; Poort et al., 2015; Resulaj et al., 2018) and in particular of CSt neurons (Xiong et al., 2015; Znamenskiy and Zador, 2013) in feature discrimination tasks.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and represents a speculative interpretation.

claim: Ablation of CT neurons impaired detection sensitivity.
source: Ablation of CT neurons, however, impaired detection sensitivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on CT neuron ablation effects.

claim: This result is consistent with the impact of cortical silencing on the sensory threshold for visually guided innate behavior mediated by the SC.
source: This result is consistent with the impact of cortical silencing on the sensory threshold for visually guided innate behavior mediated by the SC (Liang et al., 2015) and the involvement of the SC in simple orienting behaviors including voluntary licking (Rossi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CT neurons may represent the neural substrate underlying reported impairments in the perception of low-contrast stimuli following VC lesions.
source: Thus, CT neurons may represent the neural substrate underlying reported impairments in the perception of low-contrast stimuli following VC lesions (Cowey and Stoerig, 1995; Glickfeld et al., 2013; Pöppel et al., 1973; Weiskrantz et al., 1974).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to previous research.

claim: VC enhances neuronal activity in SC in response to visual stimuli, which may account, at least in part, for the deficits observed following VC lesions.
source: We show that VC enhances neuronal activity in SC in response to visual stimuli, which may account, at least in part, for the deficits observed following VC lesions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: With prolonged training, VC gradually loses its impact on behavior and on visual responses in SC, suggesting the existence of plasticity at the CT synapse or local plasticity within the SC.
source: With prolonged training, VC gradually loses its impact on behavior and on visual responses in SC, suggesting the existence of plasticity at the CT synapse or local plasticity within the SC.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Given that cortical neurons with distinct projection targets have been shown to form segregated subnetworks, the connectivity and function of the spared neurons is largely unaffected by ablation of a specific population of cortico-fugal neurons.
source: However, given that cortical neurons with distinct projection targets have been shown to form segregated subnetworks (Brown and Hestrin, 2009; Harris and Mrsic-Flogel, 2013; Kim et al., 2018; Lur et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016), we believe that the connectivity and function of the spared neurons is largely unaffected.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and represents an inference about the experimental approach.

claim: Given that, following VC lesions, the SC is the main visual processing stage in the brain and given the role of the cortico-fugal pathway targeting the dmSt in learning, a subcortical SC-basal ganglia loop may mediate the slower, VC-independent learning.
source: Given that, following VC lesions, the SC is the main visual processing stage in the brain and given the role of the cortico-fugal pathway targeting the dmSt in learning, we hypothesize that a subcortical SC-basal ganglia loop mediates the slower, VC-independent learning.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the experimental findings.

claim: A somatosensory detection task can be learned to proficiency in the absence of somatosensory cortex, possibly involving subcortical basal ganglia loops.
source: Along these lines, recent findings indicate that a somatosensory detection task can be learned to proficiency in the absence of somatosensory cortex (Hong et al., 2018), possibly involving subcortical basal ganglia loops (Bosman et al., 2011; Redgrave et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The fact that, with prolonged training, the behavior becomes independent of VC implies that the underlying subcortical structures can entirely rely on ascending sensory input from the periphery rather than on descending cortico-fugal pathways.
source: The fact that, with prolonged training, the behavior becomes independent of VC implies that the underlying subcortical structures can entirely rely on ascending sensory input from the periphery rather than on descending cortico-fugal pathways.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The gradual reduction in the role of VC on behavior may reflect a transition from goal-directed to habitual behavior.
source: The gradual reduction in the role of VC on behavior may, furthermore, reflect a transition from goal-directed to habitual behavior (Balleine, 2019; Dickinson, 1994).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to previous research.

claim: VC, through its cortico-fugal projection to the dmSt, may facilitate behavioral flexibility in an ever-changing environment during goal-directed behavior.
source: On one hand, VC, through its cortico-fugal projection to the dmSt, may facilitate behavioral flexibility in an ever-changing environment during goal-directed behavior.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The subcortical sources of visual input to the basal ganglia may be sufficient to drive habitual responses upon prolonged training in stable contingencies.
source: On the other hand, the subcortical sources of visual input to the basal ganglia may be sufficient to drive habitual responses upon prolonged training in stable contingencies.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Two distinct populations of cortico-fugal neurons in the VC that give rise to major descending projections targeting phylogenetically older subcortical structures substantially contribute to visually guided behavior of a simple detection task, by increasing learning speed and improving detection sensitivity.
source: In summary, two distinct populations of cortico-fugal neurons in the VC that give rise to major descending projections targeting phylogenetically older subcortical structures, substantially contribute to visually guided behavior of a simple detection task, by increasing learning speed and improving detection sensitivity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The improvement in learning and performance by defined classes of cortico-fugal neurons may represent an early adaptive benefit to goal-directed behavior associated with the expansion of cortex in mammals.
source: The improvement in learning and performance by defined classes of cortico-fugal neurons may represent an early adaptive benefit to goal-directed behavior associated with the expansion of cortex in mammals.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the broader implications of the findings.
